recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — give the definition as an implication, and say what you check in your example.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: State the definition
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write it as an implication with the arrow. Symmetric does not ask for every pair to be in R, only that each pair already in R has its reverse in R.
lines: Let R be a relation on a set A, that is R ⊆ A × A.
R is called symmetric if, for all a, b ∈ A,
So whenever a is related to b, b is also related to a.

recall.must_convey: That R is symmetric when (a, b) ∈ R implies (b, a) ∈ R for all a, b in A.
accept: if a b is in R then b a is also in R
every pair can be reversed and is still in the relation
a related to b implies b related to a
a b unte b a kuda undali ante symmetric
write it as an implication with the arrow

steps.why: The condition is checked only on the pairs that are already in R, so the implication form is what a marker looks for. Writing it as a plain and would force R to hold every pair of A × A.
steps.memory_tip: Symmetric means every pair can be read backwards and is still in R.
common_mistakes: Writing (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R for all a, b, which makes R the whole of A × A.
Confusing it with reflexive by writing (a, a) ∈ R.
Writing the arrow the wrong way, so nothing is required of the pairs in R.

steps.label: Check it on an example
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Reverse each pair in the list and look for it. This R is symmetric but not reflexive, since (1, 1) and (2, 2) are missing — the two properties are separate.
lines: Reverse each pair and look for it in R:
(1, 2) ∈ R and (2, 1) ∈ R;   (2, 1) ∈ R and (1, 2) ∈ R;   (3, 3) ∈ R and its reverse is itself.

lines.text: ∴ R is a symmetric relation on A.

recall.must_convey: That each pair of R is reversed and found in R, so R is symmetric.
accept: one two and two one are both there so it is symmetric
reverse every pair and check it is still in R
three three reversed is itself so it is fine
prathi pair ni reverse chesi choodali
this one is symmetric but not reflexive

steps.why: Choosing a relation that is symmetric without being reflexive shows the definition has been read as it stands. A pair such as (3, 3) is its own reverse, so it never breaks symmetry.
steps.memory_tip: A pair (a, a) is its own reverse, so it can never spoil symmetry.
common_mistakes: Adding (1, 1) and (2, 2) to R because the list appears incomplete.
Claiming (3, 3) breaks symmetry, when its reverse is the same pair.
Checking one pair and stopping before the rest of the list.
